La binomial cuenta éxitos en intentos re: The binomial counts successes in repeated attempts, and that is why it is the model for quality control: if 2 % of the parts come out defective, what is the probability that a batch of 100 contains more than five? From that come the sampling plans that decide whether a shipment is accepted or returned. It is also the model for clinical trials, where you count how many patients improve out of how many are treated.
La distribución binomial la estudió Jaco: The binomial distribution was studied by Jacob Bernoulli in their Ars Conjectandi, published in 1713, eight years after their death. That book also contains the first proof of the law of large numbers. Bernoulli spent twenty years writing it and never finished it: they were troubled by not knowing how to apply probability to “civil and moral” affairs, which is exactly the problem statistics is still trying to solve.
La distribución de una variable discreta: The distribution of a discrete variable is described by its probability function: what probability each value has. And there is one case that turns up constantly.
La fórmula se entiende sola si la lees p: The formula explains itself if you read it in parts: $p^k$ is the probability of $k$ successes, $(1-p)^{n-k}$ that of the remaining failures, and $\binom{n}{k}$ counts in how many different ways those $k$ successes can be spread among the $n$ repetitions.
